To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Monkeys can learn to control a brain machine interface that uses multiple mathematical model to extract several motor and sensory parameters from frontoparietal neural ensembles and that the learning to operate the brain machine interface is paralleled by functional cortical reorganization.
monkeys can control a robot arm by operating a closed loop BMIc that extracts multiple motor parameters from the activity of large frontoparietally distributed neuronal populations.

primates can control a BMIc that extracts multiple motor parameters (i) from the electrical signals of large neuronal ensembles, and (ii) that is capable of producing reach and grasp movements in the absence of arm movements.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of BMIc systems for primates that can provide continuous, accurate and reliable control of a robot arm by using multiple models that predict multiple motor parameters from neuronal ensemble activity.
the development of a new generation of BMIs for reaching and grasping, and the exploration of the neurophysiological mechanisms underlying BMIc operation.
the development of a closed loop brain-machine interface that can be used for the restoration of motor function in patients suffering from severe paralysis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

this work provides the first example in which a primate has learned to control a robot arm by using a closed loop BMIc to extract multiple motor parameters from neuronal ensembles in the motor cortex, and in which the BMIc was integrated into the motor and sensory cortices of the monkey.
the BMIc can be successfully operated by primates and can be used to control a robot arm for reaching and grasping virtual objects.
this study shows that primates can use a closed loop BMI to control a robotic arm and that the use of this BMI is associated with functional reorganization of multiple cortical areas.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain can be trained to operate a BMIc by learning to predict and control the dynamic properties of an external system.
the BMIc is a powerful tool to study motor learning in nonhuman primates.

we have developed and validated an advanced brain machine interface that can be operated by primates to control a virtual arm and that this BMIc can be used to study the neural basis of motor learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain has remarkable plasticity, which can be used to learn the control of complex robotic systems.
BMIc can be learned by primates and that the BMIc can be used to produce coordinated movements that are similar to those produced by the primate brain.
the brain can be trained to produce motor behavior by using BMIcs that extract motor parameters from the activity of large neuronal ensembles.
